examples.ko: 이길 방법이 없어서 새로운 계책을 세웠어요.
examples.en: There was no way to win, so we came up with a new plan.

examples.ko: 그 신하의 계책 덕분에 나라가 위기를 넘겼어요.
examples.en: Thanks to that minister's stratagem, the country got through the crisis.
I have no particular plan, and it's frustrating.
The plan is good, but it's hard to carry out.
My younger sibling racked their brain for a scheme to raise their allowance.

examples.ko: 여러 계책 끝에 겨우 문제를 풀었어요.
examples.en: After trying several tactics, I finally solved the problem.

explain: 사극이나 역사 이야기에서 많이 나오고, 일상에서는 '방법', '꾀', '수'를 더 자주 말해요. '계책을 세우다', '계책을 짜내다'처럼 같이 써요.
explain_en: It appears often in historical dramas and stories, while in daily life people more often say '방법', '꾀' or '수'. It pairs with verbs as in '계책을 세우다' (draw up a plan) and '계책을 짜내다' (rack one's brain for a scheme).

examples.ko: 올해 입시는 단념하고 내년을 준비하기로 했어요.
examples.en: I decided to give up on this year's entrance exam and prepare for next year.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 단념이 빨라서 안 되면 바로 다른 길을 찾아요.
examples.en: He gives up quickly, so if something doesn't work he looks for another path right away.

examples.ko: 어려워도 꿈을 단념하지 말고 계속 도전하세요.
examples.en: Even if it's hard, don't give up your dream and keep trying.
My parents objected, so I gave up on studying abroad.

examples.ko: 가격이 너무 비싸서 사는 것을 단념할 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.en: It was so expensive that I had no choice but to give up buying it.
He is not someone who gives up easily.

explain: '포기하다'와 비슷하지만 단념하다는 '이제 그만 생각하자' 하고 마음속에서 접는 느낌이 강해요. 일상 대화에서는 '포기하다'가 더 흔하고, 단념하다는 글이나 조금 격식 있는 말에서 자주 보여요. '~을/를 단념하다'로 써요.
explain_en: It is close to '포기하다', but 단념하다 stresses closing the matter in your own mind, telling yourself to stop thinking about it. In daily conversation '포기하다' is more common; 단념하다 appears more in writing or slightly formal speech. It is used as '~을/를 단념하다'.

examples.en: When the soup in the pot starts bubbling, turn down the heat.
When I heard that, I seethed inside.
I can hear the stew bubbling.

examples.ko: 라면 물이 부글거리기 시작하면 면을 넣으세요.
examples.en: When the ramen water starts to bubble, add the noodles.

examples.ko: 가스 때문에 배가 부글거려서 병원에 갔어요.
examples.en: My stomach was gurgling from gas, so I went to the hospital.
Bubbles are rising from the pond with a gurgling sound.

explain: '끓다'는 상태를 말하고, '부글거리다'는 거품이 올라오며 소리가 나는 모습까지 담아요. 화가 속에서 치밀 때는 '속이 부글거리다'라고 해요. '부글부글'에 '-거리다'가 붙은 말이라 '부글대다'로도 써요.
explain_en: '끓다' names the state, while '부글거리다' also carries the rising bubbles and the sound. When anger wells up inside, people say '속이 부글거리다'. It is '부글부글' plus '-거리다', and '부글대다' is used the same way.

en: risking life; being desperate; being all or nothing

examples.en: He said he would take on this match with everything on the line.
The two teams fought an all-or-nothing match.

examples.ko: 사생결단을 내서라도 이 일을 끝내야 해요.
examples.en: We have to finish this, even if it takes a do-or-die effort.
He threw himself into studying for the exam as if his life depended on it.

examples.ko: 사생결단 각오로 나서면 못 할 일이 없어요.
examples.en: If you go in with a do-or-die attitude, nothing is impossible.
In the meeting, they pushed their opinions as if it were life or death.

explain: '사생결단을 내다', '사생결단하다'처럼 써요. 시합이나 큰 승부에서 많이 쓰는 센 표현이고, 일상에서는 '죽기 살기로'를 더 편하게 써요.
explain_en: It is used as '사생결단을 내다' or '사생결단하다'. It is a rather dramatic, strong expression often used for matches and big showdowns, while '죽기 살기로' is the more casual everyday equivalent.

en: to be shameful; to be humiliating

examples.en: I'm so ashamed that my lie was found out.

examples.ko: 그는 수치스러운 기억을 잊고 싶어 해요.
examples.en: He wants to forget his humiliating memory.
It was humiliating to get it wrong in front of people.
I was so ashamed that my face turned red.
I think that kind of behavior is shameful.

examples.ko: 저는 수치스럽지 않은 삶을 살고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to live a life I'm not ashamed of.

explain: 일상에서는 '창피하다'를 훨씬 자주 쓰고, 수치스럽다는 더 무겁고 글에 가까워요. 가벼운 실수에는 '창피해요'가 자연스러워요. '부끄럽다'는 마음속에서 느끼는 감정이고, 수치스럽다는 남 앞에서 체면이 크게 상한 느낌이 강해요.
explain_en: In daily speech '창피하다' is far more common; '수치스럽다' is heavier and more bookish. For small slips, '창피해요' sounds natural. '부끄럽다' is an inner feeling, while '수치스럽다' stresses a serious loss of face in front of others.

examples.ko: 그는 한 번만 기회를 달라고 애걸했어요.
examples.en: He begged for just one chance.

examples.ko: 저는 애걸하다시피 해서 겨우 사장님을 만났어요.
examples.en: I practically begged and finally managed to meet the boss.

examples.ko: 친구에게 돈을 빌려 달라고 애걸하기는 싫어요.
examples.en: I don't want to beg my friend to lend me money.
No matter how much I begged, the teacher didn't allow it.
The child spoke as if pleading, with tears in his eyes.
You don't need to beg like that.

explain: 글이나 뉴스에서 자주 보이는 딱딱한 말이에요. 대화에서는 '빌다', '매달리다', '사정하다'처럼 말하는 일이 많아요.
explain_en: This is a fairly stiff word often seen in writing and the news. In conversation people often say '빌다', '매달리다' or '사정하다' instead.

examples.en: The employee protested that it wasn't his fault.
Protesting that I'd been wronged was useless.

examples.ko: 아이는 저도 열심히 했다고요 하고 항변하더라고요.
examples.en: The child protested, saying, I tried hard too!

examples.ko: 그는 부당한 대우에 끝까지 항변하려고 했어요.
examples.en: He tried to protest the unfair treatment to the end.

examples.ko: 소비자들이 가격 인상에 항변하는 글을 올리고 있어요.
examples.en: Consumers are posting messages protesting the price hike.

examples.ko: 항변할 기회조차 주지 않아서 화가 났어요.
examples.en: I was angry because they didn't even give me a chance to protest.

explain: '~라고 항변하다', '~에 항변하다'로 써요. 단순히 반대 의견을 말하는 '반박하다'와 달리, 억울하거나 부당하다는 마음이 담겨 있어요. 일상 대화에서는 '따지다', '억울하다고 말하다'가 더 자연스러운 경우가 많아요.
explain_en: It is used as '~라고 항변하다' or '~에 항변하다'. Unlike '반박하다' (to rebut), it carries a feeling of being wronged or treated unfairly. In everyday talk, '따지다' or '억울하다고 말하다' often sounds more natural.
